On Quantum Perceptron Learning via
Quantum Search
Xiaoyu Sun†* , Mathieu Roget†, Giuseppe Di Molfetta†, and Hachem Kadri†
Abstract—With the growing interest in quantum machine learning, the perceptron—a fundamental building block in traditional
machine learning—has emerged as a valuable model for exploring
quantum advantages. Two quantum perceptron algorithms based
on Grover’s search, were developed in [18] to accelerate training
and improve statistical efficiency in perceptron learning. This
paper points out and corrects a mistake in the proof of [18,
Theorem 2]. Specifically, we show that the probability of sampling
from a normal distribution for a D-dimensional hyperplane that
perfectly classifies the data scales as Ω(γD) instead of Θ(γ),
where γ is the margin. We then revisit two well-established linear
programming algorithms—the ellipsoid method and the cutting
plane random walk algorithm—in the context of perceptron
learning, and show how quantum search algorithms can be
leveraged to enhance the overall complexity. Specifically, both
algorithms gain a sub-linear speed-up O(
√
N) in the number of
data points N as a result of Grover’s algorithm and an additional
O(D1.5) speed-up is possible for cutting plane random walk
algorithm employing quantum walk search.
Keywords—Quantum machine learning, Linear classification,
Perceptron learning, Quantum search, Grover’s algorithm, Quantum walk.
I.
INTRODUCTION
With the great development of computational power and
algorithms, machine learning has gained more and more attention in the modern stage with the increasing demand to learn
from big data of high feature space dimension and generalize
to unseen data, which greatly motivates the use of quantum
computing in machine learning. This growing interest has
stimulated the emergence of quantum machine learning interdiscipline [3], [33].
Originating from the suggestion to use quantum hardware
to simulate quantum dynamics with exponential overhead [9],
quantum computing integrated knowledge from quantum algorithms, quantum information processing and experimental
quantum systems. There is growing interest in utilizing quantum mechanics to assist machine learning based on the following facts. First, the unique superposition property allows a
qubit to be |0⟩and |1⟩simultaneously, equipping qubit systems
with an exponentially compact representation compared to bit
systems. Classical data can be mapped to quantum states with
their probability distributions encoded into amplitudes. This
can be extremely useful in handling big data, in which the
number of features D can be in the millions. Second, quantum
operation inherits quantum parallelism naturally, which allows

the use of quantum basic linear algebra subroutines such
as quantum Fourier transform [29] and HHL algorithm [15]
that operate in polylog(D) time, or some others subroutines
with quadratic speed-up, such as Grover’s search [13] and its
extension quantum counting algorithm [5]. Third, it is argued
that since quantum mechanics can produce distributions that
are intricate to produce by classical computers, it possibly has
a stronger ability to recognize patterns [3], which could be
privileged with quantum data.
In supervised machine learning, classification requires algorithms/models to give the correct label to unseen (test) data
based on knowledge recognized from labelled training data.
The simplest task in classification is likely binary classification
on linearly separable data, which is known can be solved
by the online perceptron algorithm [32] with tight update
bound that only depends on the geometric margin of data [4],
[30]. Although the perceptron algorithm is straightforward, it
is the basic building unit of multilayer perceptron (MLP),
i.e. the single-layer perceptron, which is also the simplest
feedforward neural network (FNN). Due to its elementariness
and simplicity, it has been considered a good example to study
for potential quantum speed-ups on the training complexity and
the statistical efficiency of machine learning algorithms [18].
The rest of our paper is organized as follows: in Section II,
we review the connections between perceptron learning, version space and feasible region. We also re-examine two algorithms, online quantum perceptron and quantum version space
perceptron proposed in [18] and their extensions in [22], [31].
In Section III, we correct a mistake in the quantum version
space perceptron [18]. Specifically, the probability of sampling
for a D-dimensional hyperplane from a normal distribution
that perfectly classifies the data scales as Ω(γD) instead of
Θ(γ), with γ denoting the margin. Additionally, we provide a
simulation validating our theoretical result. In Section IV, we
show how the quantum analogues of two linear programming
algorithms —ellipsoidal algorithm and cutting plane random
walk algorithm can be used to speed up perceptron learning
under a weak online learning setup. Section V provides a
cutting plane quantum hit-and-run algorithm, elaborating on
how to use quantum walk search [25] to further speed up
sampling. Section VI concludes the paper and also discusses
the possibility of acquiring statistical advantages in quantum
machine learning.
II.

Now, given N normalized linearly separable training examples {x1, ., xN} ∈RD, ||xi|| = 1,2 with corresponding

is a weight vector (hyperplane) that follows a prediction rule
ˆyi = sgn(wT xi) for every unlabelled instance xi.3 Perceptron
learning aims to find a hyperplane wT xiyi > 0, ∀i ∈[N],
such that the perceptron solution has the correct prediction on
every example. In the parameter space, the set of hyperplanes
satisfying all these N inequalities is called version space
VS := {w | wT xiyi > 0, ∀i ∈[N]}. As only directions of w
matter for classification, we can limit the length of ||w|| ≤1.
Geometrically, the VS is a bounded polyhedron (a polytope)
satisfying N half-spaces constraints, which is also known as a
feasible set in the context of convex optimization. When training into converge, the well-known perceptron algorithm [32]
yields a point inside the VS, and the SVM solution is the centre
of the largest radius sphere that can be embedded into the
VS [35]. Noticing the connections between version space and
the feasibility problem, we are interested in exploring methods
other than the perceptron algorithm to achieve the same goal
of perceptron learning.

IV.
LINEAR PROGRAMMING ALGORITHMS IN QUANTUM
Setting
Now, we move to the section where we discuss the
linear programming algorithms in the quantum setting. We
consider two algorithms: the ellipsoid method and the cutting
plane random walk algorithm. Both algorithms gain a sub-linear
speed-up O(√N) in the number of data points N as a result of
Grover’s algorithm and an additional O(D1.5) speed-up is
possible for cutting plane random walk algorithm employing
quantum walk search.
A. Ellipsoid Method
The ellipsoid method is an iterative algorithm for convex
optimization. It starts with an initial ellipsoid containing the
optimal solution and iteratively shrinks the ellipsoid by cutting
it with a hyperplane at each step. The algorithm terminates when
the ellipsoid is small enough to contain the optimal solution.

B. Cutting Plane Random Walk Algorithm
The cutting plane random walk algorithm is a probabilistic
approach for solving convex optimization problems. It starts
with a random point within the feasible region and iteratively
adds cutting planes that shave off parts of the feasible region
until the desired accuracy is achieved.

C. Grover’s Algorithm and Quantum Walk Search
We employ Grover’s algorithm to speed up the search for
certain states, and quantum walk search to further speed up the
sampling process. The quantum walk search is used in the
cutting plane random walk algorithm to enhance the speed at
which the hyperplanes are added.

V.
CUTTING PLANE QUANTUM HIT-AND-RUN ALGORITHM
In this section, we introduce a cutting plane quantum
hit-and-run algorithm, elaborating on how to use quantum
walk search to further speed up the sampling. The quantum
hit-and-run algorithm is a variant of the classical hit-and-run
algorithm, which is a Markov chain Monte Carlo method for
sampling uniformly from a convex body. The quantum version
allows for faster sampling by leveraging quantum walks to
explore the state space more efficiently.

A. Quantum Walk Search
The quantum walk search is a technique that uses quantum
mechanics to enhance the performance of classical algorithms
that rely on random sampling. It is particularly useful in
settings where the classical algorithms can be represented as
a Markov chain, and the quantum walk can be used to speed up
the mixing time of the chain.

B. Hit-and-Run Algorithm
The hit-and-run algorithm is a Markov chain Monte Carlo
method for sampling uniformly from a convex body. It works by
selecting a random direction and "hitting" the boundary of the
body in that direction, then "running" along the direction until
it reaches the opposite boundary.

C. Quantum Hit-and-Run Algorithm
The quantum hit-and-run algorithm is an adaptation of the
classical hit-and-run algorithm that uses quantum walks to
sample points from the convex body more efficiently. In the
quantum version, the walk is performed on the state space of
the convex body, allowing for faster exploration and mixing
of the states.

D. Hybrid Model with Quantum Walk Search
By combining the quantum walk search with the classical
hit-and-run algorithm, we develop a hybrid model that further
speeds up the sampling process. The quantum walk is used to
explore the state space, while the hit-and-run algorithm ensures
uniform coverage of the convex body.

VI.
CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this paper, we have presented several quantum algorithms
for perceptron learning, including the online quantum perceptron
and quantum version space perceptron. We corrected a mistake
in the quantum version space perceptron by showing that the
probability of sampling a hyperplane from a normal distribution
that perfectly classifies the data scales as Ω(γD) instead of
Θ(γ). We also explored the use of quantum walk search in
the cutting plane algorithms for perceptron learning, achieving
sub-linear speed-ups on the number of data points and additional
speed-ups based on the dimensionality of the data.

Future work includes extending these results to other
machine learning models, such as support vector machines and
